content: Sepsis is a condition that arises when an infection leads to organ failure. In some cases, sepsis may be associated with impaired corticosteroid metabolism, which has led to the hypothesis that administering corticosteroids could be beneficial for these patients. This review, originally published in 2004 and updated in 2010 and 2015, was further updated to evaluate the effects of corticosteroids on mortality in children and adults with sepsis. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN, and the WHO Clinical Trials Search Portal, on July 25, 2019. Additional studies were identified through reference checking, citation searching, and direct contact with study authors. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing corticosteroids to placebo or usual care (which included antimicrobials, fluid replacement, and vasopressor therapy as needed) in children and adults with sepsis. Trials comparing continuous infusion versus intermittent bolus administration of corticosteroids were also included. The review process involved screening and selecting studies, extracting data, and assessing the methodological quality of the trials. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Authors of the review did not assess eligibility, risk of bias, or extract data for trials in which they had participated. A total of 61 trials involving 12,192 participants were included in the review. Of these, six trials exclusively involved children, two included both children and adults, and the remaining trials focused solely on adults. Nine additional studies are ongoing and will be considered in future updates. Nineteen trials were judged to have a low risk of bias. When comparing corticosteroids to placebo or usual care, the findings were as follows: Corticosteroids probably slightly reduce 28-day mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.91, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84 to 0.99; moderate-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids may result in little to no difference in long-term mortality (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.03; low-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids probably slightly reduce hospital mortality (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.99; moderate-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids significantly reduced the length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU) (mean difference [MD] -1.07 days, 95% CI -1.95 to -0.19; high-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids also resulted in a substantial reduction in the length of hospital stay (MD -1.63 days, 95% CI -2.93 to -0.33; high-certainty evidence). However, corticosteroids were associated with certain adverse effects: They increased the risk of muscle weakness (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.44; high-certainty evidence). They increased the risk of hypernatraemia (high-certainty evidence). They probably increased the risk of hyperglycaemia (moderate-certainty evidence). Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that corticosteroids probably do not increase the risk of superinfection (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.19). There was probably little or no difference in the risk of gastroduodenal bleeding, stroke, or cardiac events (moderate-certainty evidence). Low-certainty evidence suggested that corticosteroids may result in little to no difference in neuropsychiatric events. Regarding the comparison between continuous infusion and intermittent bolus administration of corticosteroids, the evidence was very uncertain. Only three studies reported data for this comparison, and the certainty of the evidence for all outcomes was very low. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence indicates that corticosteroids probably reduce 28-day and hospital mortality in patients with sepsis. High-certainty evidence shows that corticosteroids significantly reduce the length of ICU and hospital stays. While there may be little or no difference in the risk of major complications, corticosteroids increase the risk of muscle weakness and hypernatraemia and probably increase the risk of hyperglycaemia. The effects of continuous infusion versus intermittent bolus administration of corticosteroids remain uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence.
